title: Matthew 27:1–2
context: After the night trial and Peter’s denial (ch. 26), morning comes. The chief priests and elders take formal counsel to put Jesus to death, then bind Him and deliver Him over to Pontius Pilate the governor.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Classic Arminian and Reformed comment on Matthew 27:1–2, in the writers’ own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: In the morning - As the sanhedrim used to meet in one of the courts of the temple, which was never opened in the night, they were forced to stay till the morning before they could proceed regularly, in the resolution they had taken to put him to death. Having bound him - They had bound him when he was first apprehended.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 27:1–2)

reformed.quote: The high priest, with his council, after having examined him at an unseasonable hour of the night, finally resolve, at sunrise, to place him at the bar of the governor. By so doing, they observe the form of judicial proceedings, that they may not be suspected of undue haste, when they run to Pilate at an unusually early hour, as usually happens in cases of tumult.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 27:1–2)

verses.text: Now when morning had come, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death.
verses.arminianNotes:
Morning light does not soften their aim. The council that plotted by stealth now takes counsel to kill. Matthew shows deliberation, not a momentary flare of anger.

One hears accountable choice under revealed light. These leaders had heard Jesus’ teaching and seen His works; grace that invites does not erase the gravity of resolving His death. Human freedom remains authentic—and responsible.
verses.reformedNotes:
The Passion advances on schedule: morning, counsel, death as the stated end. What they feared to do during the feast (26:5) they now pursue in daylight.

Culpable counsel and sovereign purpose. God is not the author of their murderous intent, yet this morning sits inside the delivering-up Jesus already named. Wicked hands move; the Father’s plan is not derailed.

verses.text: They bound him, led him away, and delivered him up to Pontius Pilate, the governor.
verses.arminianNotes:
Bound, led, delivered: the Holy One is handed to Rome. Religious leaders refuse to finish the deed alone; they enlist Gentile power. Jesus does not break free; He goes as the Lamb who yields Himself.

The delivering is actual history and a sincere call to trust the suffering Christ. Grace enables faith that follows a bound Savior rather than a Messiah of force. Hearers remain responsible for how they receive this path.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Delivered… over to Pilate” fulfills the language of handing over. Bound yet not defeated, Jesus enters the governor’s jurisdiction so the cross will be public and juridical, not a quiet lynching.

The Son is delivered according to purpose, not as a victim of chance. Pilate’s authority is not in doubt; Christ’s mission is deeper. The church confesses a Lord who was led away without His Father’s will being overturned.
verses.keyContrast: Both refuse a helpless accident. Arminians stress Jesus’ knowing self-giving and a sincere summons to trust the bound Christ; Reformed readers stress that this delivering-over advances the Father’s appointed purpose without excusing the priests’ guilt.
